title: Part 1: Poetry — Foregrounding & Deviation
description: Comprehensive study of Poetic Licence, Parallelism, and all levels of linguistic deviation.

lessons.title: Basic Concepts & Poetic Licence
lessons.subtitle: The rules of Stylistics and the freedom of the poet.

content.heading: Theory: Poetic Licence (الرخصة الشعرية)
content.body:
Poetic Licence: It is the poet's right to ignore rules and conventions generally observed by users of the language to achieve artistic effects.

الرخصة الشعرية: هي حق الشاعر في تجاهل القواعد اللغوية المتعارف عليها لتحقيق أغراض جمالية أو فنية.

content.heading: Applied: Breaking the Rules
content.body: Example from Gerard Manley Hopkins: 'The just man justices.'

steps.label: Observation
steps.body: Standard grammar uses 'justice' as a noun. Hopkins converts it into a verb ('justices').

steps.label: Analysis
steps.body: This is Functional Conversion (Syntactic Deviation). It emphasizes the active, living nature of justice rather than it being a static concept.

content.heading: Theory: Levels of Language
content.body: Stylistics analyzes language at three fundamental levels:

steps.label: Realization
steps.body: Sounds (Phonology) and Marks on paper (Graphology).

steps.label: Form
steps.body: Words (Lexicon) and Grammar (Syntax).

steps.label: Meaning
steps.body: The ultimate semantic interpretation.

lessons.title: Foregrounding & Parallelism
lessons.subtitle: Methods of making text stand out.

content.heading: Theory: Foregrounding (البروز الأسلوبي)
content.body: Refers to the ways in which certain aspects of a text can be made to stand out or appear prominent through forms of textual patterning.

content.heading: Theory: Parallelism (الموازنة)
content.body: Extra regular use of a linguistic feature. It pushes readers towards perceiving semantic relations between words which do not exist as such in the language system.

steps.label: Identity
steps.body: Part of the structure stays constant.

steps.label: Contrast
steps.body: Specific words are changed to create new associations.

content.heading: Applied: Analyzing Parallelism
content.body: Passage: 'Where wealth accumulates and men decay.' (Oliver Goldsmith)

steps.label: Structure
steps.body: Noun + Verb vs Noun + Verb.

steps.label: Contrast
steps.body: Wealth (Material) vs Men (Humanity). Accumulates (Growth) vs Decay (Decline).

steps.label: Effect
steps.body: The poet forces a link between the increase of wealth and the destruction of the human soul.

steps.label: Semantic (Metaphor)
steps.body: 'Death feeds on his mute voice...' (Personification of Death).

steps.label: Syntactic (Inversion)
steps.body: 'Her Kindling buds as if she Autumn were.' (Word order reversed).

steps.label: Lexical (Poetic Compound)
steps.body: 'The passion-winged ministers of thought.' (Newly created compound).

steps.label: Phonological (Syncope)
steps.body: 'o'er' instead of 'over' (Omission of medial sounds).

steps.label: Graphological
steps.body: Splitting words like 'H-E-L-L' vertically to force separate pronunciation.

title: Part 2: Novel — Cohesion
description: How sentences are woven together through Reference, Ellipsis, Conjunction, and Lexical ties.

lessons.title: Kinds of Cohesion
lessons.subtitle: The linguistic means by which sentences are tied together.

content.heading: Theory: Cohesion (السبك)
content.body: The linguistic elements that tie a text together across sentence boundaries.

content.heading: Theory: 4 Types of Cohesion
content.body: Cohesion is achieved through four main grammatical and lexical methods:

steps.label: Reference
steps.body: Using pronouns or demonstratives (He, This, That).

steps.label: Ellipsis
steps.body: Omitting repeated elements ('I like tea, and she [likes] coffee').

steps.label: Conjunctions
steps.body: Logical connectors (And, But, Because, Then).

steps.label: Lexical Cohesion
steps.body: Reiteration (Repetition, Synonymy, Hyponymy) and Collocation.

steps.label: Repetition
steps.body: 'Justice... Justice... Justice' used repeatedly.

steps.label: Hyponymy
steps.body: 'Rose' is a hyponym of the category 'Flower'.

steps.label: Collocation
steps.body: 'Strong tea' or 'Bread and butter' (words that naturally go together).

content.heading: Applied: Identifying Reference
content.body: How do pronouns point to things?

steps.label: Anaphoric
steps.body: 'John arrived. He was tired.' (He points back to John).

steps.label: Cataphoric
steps.body: 'When he arrived, John was tired.' (He points forward to John).

steps.label: Exophoric
steps.body: 'Look at that!' (That points to something in the physical world).

title: Part 3: Narrative Structure
description: Labov's 6 elements and the art of internal evaluation.

lessons.title: Labov's 6 Elements
lessons.subtitle: The skeleton of any well-formed story.

content.heading: Theory: Narrative Structure
content.body: A narrative is a text in which something humanly interesting has happened, consisting of 6 specific parts.

content.heading: Theory & Applied: The 6 Parts
content.body: Let's apply the theory to a mini-story:

steps.label: 1. Abstract
steps.body: Summary: 'Let me tell you about the time I almost died.'

steps.label: 2. Orientation
steps.body: Context: 'I was in Cairo last summer with my family.'

steps.label: 3. Complicating Action
steps.body: Events: 'A car swerved towards us and I jumped out of the way.'

steps.label: 4. Evaluation
steps.body: Significance: 'I was so terrified, I thought it was the end.'

steps.label: 5. Resolution
steps.body: Outcome: 'The car missed us and we were safe.'

steps.label: 6. Coda
steps.body: Bridge to present: 'And that is why I never cross that street anymore.'

title: Part 4: Dialogue and Drama
description: Politeness Strategies, Grice's Maxims, and the Birmingham Model.

content.heading: Theory: Positive & Negative Face
content.body: Positive Face: Your desire to be liked/approved. Negative Face: Your desire to be free from imposition.

steps.label: Positive Politeness
steps.body: 'What a fantastic garden you have.' (Compliment to build rapport).

steps.label: Negative Politeness
steps.body: 'Could you find me a computer?' (Hedged request to respect freedom).

steps.label: Negative Politeness
steps.body: 'Sorry to bother you. I couldn’t borrow $30, could I...?' (Apology + indirectness).

steps.label: Off-record
steps.body: 'Oh, I'm so stupid, I forgot my wallet.' (Hinting without a direct request).

content.heading: Theory & Applied: Flouted Maxims
content.body: When we break rules to imply hidden meanings:

steps.label: Maxim of Relevance
steps.body: A: 'Weather prediction?' B: 'Bring your coat.' (Implication: It will rain/be cold).

steps.label: Maxim of Quantity
steps.body: Hamlet: 'Words, words, words.' (Too vague/uninformative).

steps.label: Maxim of Manner
steps.body: Using obscure language to avoid being direct.

title: Part 5: Modality
description: Expressing opinion and attitude through probability, obligation, willingness, and usuality.

content.heading: Theory: Modality
content.body: The linguistic means for qualifying any claim or commitment you make in language.

steps.label: Probability
steps.body: 'He might fall.' vs 'He must fall.'

steps.label: Obligation
steps.body: 'You should see a doctor.' vs 'You must see a doctor.'

lessons.title: Applied: The Kite Runner
lessons.subtitle: Analysis of Modality and Evaluative Devices.

content.heading: Applied: Kite Runner Analysis
content.body: Passage: 'Afghanistan is the land of Pashtuns. It always has been, always will be, we are the true Afghans, the pure Afghans.'

steps.label: Modality (Usuality)
steps.body: The use of 'Always' ('always has been, always will be') expresses high certainty and inevitability. It presents the speaker's claim as an inescapable truth.

steps.label: Categorical Assertion
steps.body: The use of the present simple 'is/are' stresses that this is a fact in the speaker's view, allowing no room for doubt.

steps.label: Evaluative Devices
steps.body: Adjectives like 'true' and 'pure' show a highly positive evaluation of the speaker's own race (Pashtuns), revealing prejudice and self-conceit.
